PLANT GUIDE · SWISS CHEESE VINE

Monstera adansonii

Monstera adansonii Schott — the Swiss cheese vine

A young vine already wearing its windows: oval leaves punched with neat elliptical holes that stay inside the blade, growing in clay pebbles in a pot painted like a festival. The leaves are pale lime because they are young and the light is strong — give this one something to climb and the green deepens as the leaves size up.

🔍 Anatomy — Holes That Stay Home

ADANSONII — holes stay
inside the blade
OBLIQUA — more hole
than leaf (not yours)
RHAPHIDOPHORA — splits cut
to the edge (not yours)

Three look-alikes, one decisive test. Your plant’s holes are closed ovals enclosed in the leaf — that alone rules out Rhaphidophora tetrasperma (the “mini monstera”), whose divisions are splits that cut all the way to the margin. And there is far too much leaf: tissue clearly outweighs holes, which rules out the true Monstera obliqua — a paper-thin rarity that is more hole than leaf and barely grows. Yours is Monstera adansonii. The long holes running close to the midrib, several breaking out to the edge, lean toward the form sold as ‘Laniata’ (botanically subsp. laniata) — a lean, not a verdict; the trade name is used loosely.

🧀 About that pale color. No cream sectors, no marbling — this is not variegation. Uniform chartreuse on a young plant under bright light is youth plus light. Botanists think the holes themselves let wind pass through and light reach the leaves below. If fully mature leaves stay pale, check the feeding — in LECA there is no soil to feed from.

🌤️ Conditions — Born to Climb

In the wild this is a hemiepiphyte: it starts on the forest floor and climbs the nearest tree trunk, and the higher it climbs, the bigger and holier its leaves get. That one fact runs the whole care plan — a moss pole isn’t decoration for this plant, it’s the difference between a trailing vine of small leaves and a climber with leaves a foot long. Trailing from a shelf is fine too; just expect the leaves to stay small.

🪴 Care Card

☀️ LightBright indirect, ~10,000–20,000 lux (about 1,000–2,000 foot-candles). More light = bigger leaves with more holes; direct midday sun scorches.
💧 Water — LECAYours grows in clay pebbles: keep the reservoir about one-third of the pot, top up as it falls, and flush under the tap monthly to wash out salt buildup. In soil instead: water when the top 1–2 inches dry.
🌱 FeedingPebbles hold no food, so LECA plants need it in the water — a weak balanced hydroponic feed at most waterings. In soil, feed every 2–4 weeks in the growing season; rest in winter.
🧗 SupportGive it a moss pole and tie the stem gently as it climbs — aerial roots gripping the pole are what trigger the big mature leaves. Or let it trail, small-leaved and happy.
🌡️ ColdHappy at 65–85°F; keep above 55–60°F and away from drafts — cold-stalled adansonii sulks and yellows.
🪴 MediumLECA: rinse the pebbles and refresh the top layer yearly. Soil: a chunky aroid mix — bark, perlite, a little coir — never dense potting soil.

🌱 Propagation & Troubleshooting

  1. Cut below a node — a stem piece with one leaf and, ideally, an aerial root.
  2. Root it in water, damp moss, or straight into LECA; bright indirect light, 65–80°F.
  3. Roots in 2–4 weeks. Pot on at 2 inches of root — or pin nodes to a pole and let the plant propagate itself upward.
💚 Stays paleYoung leaves harden off deeper green. If mature leaves stay lime, feed more (LECA) or ease back from the brightest spot.
🍃 Small, hole-less leavesJuvenile growth or low light. Brighten it and give it a pole — holes arrive as leaves size up.
🕷️ ThripsThe signature pest of this plant: silvery speckle, black dots, distorted new leaves. Shower, isolate, insecticidal soap weekly until clear.
💛 YellowingStale LECA reservoir or soggy soil. Flush the pebbles; in soil, check the roots before watering again.
🦵 Leggy, long gapsReaching for light. Move brighter; prune tips to force branching, root the cuttings.
🐈
Not safe for animals. The ASPCA lists the genus Monstera as toxic to cats — insoluble calcium oxalate crystals — and NC State Extension lists M. adansonii itself. Chewing brings mouth pain, drooling, and vomiting. Keep it climbing out of reach. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.
